About the Medical Terminology event

Medical Terminology is a Health Science event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing.

Ten connected lessons cover the 2026–27 word-part and body-system blueprint. Build, compare, and translate medical language, then apply it in a written-response checkpoint. Use the official references for authoritative definitions and spelling.

Medical Terminology lessons

Unit 1 · Build precise medical language

Roots, prefixes, suffixes, spelling, and body orientation.

  1. Word roots, suffixes, and the logic of a medical term 25 min

    A procedure list contains gastrectomy, gastrotomy, and gastrostomy. The shared beginning points to the same organ, but the endings describe very different actions. Accurate decoding depends on preserving both pieces.

  2. Prefixes, opposites, plurals, and spelling traps 25 min

    Hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia differ by only a few letters. Those letters reverse the direction of the finding. A precise reader pays attention to modifiers before deciding what the term means.

  3. Anatomical position, body planes, cavities, and organization 25 min

    A note describes a lesion on the anterior left forearm. Turning the patient over does not move the lesion to a new anatomical side. Standard orientation lets different observers describe the same location.

Unit 2 · Support, movement, and circulation

Skin, skeleton, muscle, blood, and lymphatic terminology.

  1. Skin, membranes, and skeletal terminology 25 min

    A referral mentions erythema, an abrasion, and a possible fracture. Each word describes a different category of finding. The language of skin and bone becomes clearer when structure and damage are separated.

  2. Muscle, movement, and functional impairment 25 min

    Two patients have difficulty walking: one has myalgia, while another has ataxia. The words point to pain in one case and coordination in the other. Function must be described precisely before its cause is considered.

  3. Cardiovascular, blood, and lymphatic language 25 min

    A pulmonary artery carries blood toward the lungs with relatively little oxygen. It is still an artery. Vessel names depend on the direction of flow, showing why anatomy is more dependable than a memorized color.

Unit 3 · Exchange and elimination

Respiratory, digestive, and urinary pathways.

  1. Respiratory passages, gas exchange, and breathing findings 25 min

    Dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia can occur together, but they do not mean the same thing. One describes the experience of breathing, another its rate, and another oxygen in the blood.

  2. Digestive and urinary pathways: similar words, different routes 25 min

    Ureter and urethra differ by a few letters but connect different locations. Tracing a substance through the body gives each word a place and makes these distinctions easier to remember.

Unit 4 · Regulation, senses, and reproduction

Neural, endocrine, and reproductive vocabulary in context.

  1. Nervous-system and special-sense vocabulary 25 min

    Aphasia, paresis, and paresthesia may appear in the same neurological record. They concern language, strength, and sensation respectively. Similar-looking words should not erase different functions.

  2. Endocrine and reproductive language in clinical context 25 min

    A hysterectomy does not by definition remove the ovaries, and diabetes insipidus is not another name for diabetes mellitus. Shared roots and familiar labels must be checked against anatomy and accepted definitions.

Sample Medical Terminology questions

1. What does lymphadenopathy mean?

  1. Disease or enlargement of the lymph nodes
  2. Inflammation of the lymph vessels
  3. Removal of a lymph node
  4. Swelling caused by lymph fluid
Show answer

A. Disease or enlargement of the lymph nodes

Lymph/o + aden/o (gland) + -pathy (disease) refers to lymph node disease, often seen as swollen nodes. Inflamed vessels are lymphangitis, removal is lymphadenectomy, and lymph swelling is lymphedema.

2. The term myasthenia gravis contains the suffix -asthenia. What does it mean?

  1. Tension or tone
  2. Weakness or lack of strength
  3. Paralysis
  4. Wasting
Show answer

B. Weakness or lack of strength

-asthenia means weakness. Myasthenia gravis is a disorder causing muscle weakness. Tone is -tonia, paralysis is -plegia, and wasting is atrophy.

3. Which term describes inflammation of the inner lining of the heart?

  1. Pericarditis
  2. Endocarditis
  3. Myocarditis
  4. Epicarditis
Show answer

B. Endocarditis

Endo- means within, so the endocardium is the inner lining of the heart. Peri- (around) refers to the sac around the heart, myo- to the heart muscle, and epi- to the outer layer.
